stem: A 19-year-old college student comes to the emergency department due to a 1-week history of malaise, fever, and a painful right knee that he says, "I probably just hurt playing football." He has no other symptoms and reports that he has been studying hard and looking forward to an upcoming football game. The patient has a history of depression that is currently treated with fluoxetine. His family history is significant for diabetes mellitus in his father. Temperature is 38.3 C (100.9 F), blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, pulse is 108/min, and respirations are 12/min. Physical examination shows a swollen, hot right knee joint that is tender to palpation with a restricted range of motion. The patient is informed about the need for a joint aspiration for possible septic arthritis but refuses, saying, "I prefer not to have anything done with needles; I'll take pain medication and just get some rest." The physician counsels him about the risks, benefits, and alternatives to the aspiration and explains that he can be given a local anesthetic to numb the pain. The patient reports understanding the information but continues to refuse the procedure. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Admit the patient to the hospital involuntarily as untreated septic arthritis is potentially life- threatening
options.B: Allow the patient to leave, but counsel him that he can return at any time
options.C: Allow the patient to leave but inform his coach that he should not play football
options.D: Obtain a psychiatry consult to assess the patient's depression and his capacity to refuse treatment
options.E: Tell the patient that his parents must be informed because he is refusing a necessary procedure

explanations.A: If the situation is an emergency and a patient is incapacitated and cannot make a decision (eg, is unconscious), presumed consent is enough to proceed. However, if a patient has decision-making capacity, this must be respected.
explanations.B: There is a very high probability that this patient has septic arthritis, and joint aspiration and fluid analysis are essential to correctly diagnose and treat him. If he refuses the procedure, the first step is to address any issues regarding why he does not want to proceed.
explanations.C: This patient is not a minor and has a right to confidentiality; threatening to call his parents or calling his coach without permission is unethical and a violation of the physician-patient relationship. The parents or coach could be contacted with permission of the patient.
explanations.D: Apsychiatry consult would be indicated if the physician believed that the patient's depression could affect his decision-making capacity. However, this patient's depression is adequately treated with medication and there is no evidence that it is influencing his decision.
explanations.E: This patient is not a minor and has a right to confidentiality; threatening to call his parents or calling his coach without permission is unethical and a violation of the physician-patient relationship. The parents or coach could be contacted with permission of the patient.

generalExplanation: There is a very high probability that this patient has septic arthritis, and joint aspiration and fluid analysis are essential to correctly diagnose and treat him. If he refuses the procedure, the first step is to address any issues regarding why he does not want to proceed. If the patient still refuses, he should be allowed to leave based on the principle of autonomy. Patients who have decision-making capacity (are able to understand the risks and benefits of treatment and express a choice) have the right to refuse treatment. The physician should still offer the services and inform the patient that he can always return for diagnosis and treatment.
educationalObjective: Patients who have decision-making capacity have the right to refuse procedures and treatment. The physician should address any modifiable obstacles to treatment. If the patient still refuses, services should be offered if the patient reconsiders.

stem: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother due to worsening grades and repeated absences from school associated with frequent stomachaches. Her mother says, "She never had a problem before starting middle school 6 months ago. She used to walk to elementary school, but the middle school is farther away. Now, I have to take her to school myself because she refuses to get on the bus. As soon as we get close to the school, her stomach hurts and she says she's going to vomit. If she goes to school, she calls during every break to see if I'm okay. I keep telling her that I'm fine." The patient is worried that her mother will have an accident and not be able to pick her up from school and says, "I won't know what happened to her." The patient denies problems with her appetite or energy levels but has trouble concentrating in class because she is worried about getting to the phone in her locker. She denies being bullied or having other issues at school. Family history is significant for cardiovascular disease and anxiety in her father and obsessive-compulsive disorder in her maternal aunt. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Adjustment disorder develops as a response to a stressful event and causes impairment in functioning. However, adjustment disorder is not diagnosed when the patient's condition is better explained by amore specific disorder (eg, in this case, separation anxiety).
explanations.B: In dependent personality disorder, fears of separation are due to an excessive need to be taken care of, with difficulty being alone and making decisions. This patient, however, is resisting separation due to a fear of something happening to her mother. Personality disorders are not commonly diagnosed in children, whose personalities are still developing.
explanations.C: Generalized anxiety disorder involves excessive worries about multiple issues, which is not the case with this patient. Her anxiety is focused on separation.
explanations.D: Preoccupation with safety and checking behaviors can be seen in obsessive-compulsive disorder. However, this girl's behavior is due to her fear of separation from her mother, making separation anxiety the central issue.
explanations.E: This patient's fear of separation with excessive concern that something bad will happen and reluctance to leave her mother are suggestive of separation anxiety disorder. It is more common in children under age 12 but can occur at any age.
explanations.F: In somatic symptom disorder, patients are preoccupied with their somatic symptoms, with concern that they could have a serious illness. In contrast, in separation anxiety disorder, physical symptoms (eg, stomachaches, hyperventilation, headaches) occur only when separation is anticipated. Unlike someone with somatic symptom disorder, this patient does not exhibit excessive preoccupation with —hersymptoms.

generalExplanation: This patient's fear of separation with excessive concern that something bad will happen and reluctance to leave her mother are suggestive of separation anxiety disorder. It is more common in children under age 12 but can occur at any age. Some degree of separation anxiety is normal at age 9-18 months. This anxiety commonly recurs when children start school or transition in some way. In this case, the girl has to travel farther away from home to attend middle school, which has precipitated her anxiety. In children and adolescents, separation anxiety is often associated with somatic symptoms (eg, stomachaches), nightmares, and difficulty sleeping and may lead to school avoidance, as seen in this patient. In adults, separation anxiety may represent a persistent disorder from childhood or can develop suddenly, especially after a traumatic or life-changing event. Separation anxiety becomes pathological when it is persistent, impedes a child's development, or causes significant functional impairment.

stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the office for a psychiatric evaluation at his mother's insistence. She is worried that her son has no close friends, does not date, and shows no interest in activities popular with young adults. His mother describes normal developmental milestones but says, "I thought he would outgrow his shyness, but he seems more isolated than ever." The patient attends a local university where he studies engineering and performs well academically. After class, he returns home and enjoys playing computer games or reading comic books. When interviewed alone, the patient makes limited eye contact. He gives brief responses and appears somewhat anxious and uncomfortable at times, but his affect is predominantly flat. In response to questioning about reasons for avoiding social activities, he replies, "I'm just not comfortable around people. I don't like it when people try to get too personal and would rather keep to myself." This patient's behavior is most consistent with which of the following?

explanations.A: Antisocial personality disorder involves a pattern of violation of the rights of others and a lack of remorse.
explanations.B: Differentiating schizoid personality disorder from mild forms of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) can be difficult. However, a diagnosis of ASD requires both social communication deficits and repetitive/restrictive behaviors with early childhood onset. This patient's normal developmental milestones and lack of stereotyped behaviors are more consistent with schizoid personality disorder.
explanations.C: In contrast to those with schizoid personality disorder, individuals with avoidant personality disorder or social anxiety disorder desire relationships but avoid them due to fears of rejection or being embarrassed.
explanations.D: Social isolation is also seen in schizotypal and paranoid personality disorders. stem: A 43-year-old woman comes to the office due to a painful and swollen knee sustained when she tripped while walking outside her home. She blames her injury on "bad energy" that she was getting from her next- door neighbor, whom she believes does not like her. The patient thinks she "has a sixth sense" to detect "negative people" but does not believe there is any specific plot to harm her. She has worked for many years sorting items in a used clothing store and lives alone, saying, "I prefer it this way." Medical history is significant for glucose intolerance and vitamin D insufficiency. The patient has been prescribed vitamin D supplements but prefers not to take them because "one can never be sure what could be in these things." Vital signs are normal. Physical examination is significant for a painful, swollen right knee with normal range of movement. On mental status examination, it is noted that the patient is dressed in multiple layers of mismatched clothing. She has flat affect and makes limited eye contact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Diagnosis of schizotypal personality disorder requires ruling out psychotic disorders that are characterized by persistent delusions and/or hallucinations. Delusional disorder is typically characterized by fixed, delusional beliefs. Individuals with schizophrenia exhibit delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech and behavior, and negative symptoms. Although this patient has a flat affect, her odd beliefs are not held with delusional intensity, and she lacks other prominent psychotic symptoms.
explanations.B: Individuals with paranoid personality disorder demonstrate a pervasive pattern of suspiciousness and distrust. They do not exhibit eccentric behavior, magical thinking, or odd beliefs with nonparanoid themes.
explanations.C: Individuals with schizoid personality disorder are socially detached or "loners." Although they also often lack close friends, they do not have odd thinking or perceptual distortions.

Magical thinking (eg, superstition, clairvoyance), suspiciousness, and paranoid ideation can occur but are not of delusional proportions, as in psychotic disorders. educationalObjective: Schizotypal personality disorder is characterized by a long-standing pattern of eccentric behaviors and social anxiety despite familiarity. stem: A 16-year-old girl comes to the office for psychiatric follow-up accompanied by her mother. The patient has a history of depression and was started on fluoxetine 2 weeks ago. Her energy and appetite have improved, but she still struggles with feelings of sadness and low self-esteem. She has difficulty fitting in with social groups at school and tends to keep to herself. The patient's depression was diagnosed at age 14 after she attempted suicide by an overdose of 15 acetaminophen tablets. At that time, she was being sexually abused by a friend of the family; the abuse has since stopped. She also has a history of cutting behavior and self-induced vomiting. The patient uses marijuana and alcohol and has tried cocaine twice but did not like it. Family history is significant for depression in her mother and suicide in her father. The patient has had fleeting thoughts that she would be "better off dead" and "wonders how people would feel if I were gone," but she has had no suicidal intent or suicide plan. Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for suicide in this patient?

explanations.A: Family history of suicide and personal history of cutting behavior, depression, sexual abuse, and social isolation are all lesser risk factors.
explanations.B: Family history of suicide and personal history of cutting behavior, depression, sexual abuse, and social isolation are all lesser risk factors.

stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the office for a routine annual examination and is accompanied by his wife. He has no new medical problems, and the physical examination is unremarkable. At the end of the visit, the patient's wife asks to speak with the physician and expresses concern that her husband was recently placed on probation for poor work performance. Over the past few years, the patient has become increasingly irritable and less interested in his work as an insurance agent. She says, "He misses work at least once a week because he stays up all night playing poker online and then sleeps in during the day. He talks nonstop about his betting strategies and how clever they are." The patient has lost a lot of money, and they have started borrowing from her parents to pay the bills. The patient denies that he has any problems and says, "I've just been a little down these past few weeks. I know I can be on top again if I just get out of this slump. I'm one of the best poker players around." Which of the following is the best explanation for this patient's behavior?

options.A: Adjustment disorder with disturbance of emotions and conduct I

explanations.A: Adjustment disorder is characterized by emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor that has occurred within the past 3 months. Although this patient has the recent stressor of being placed on probation at work, there is evidence that he has had problematic gambling behaviors for several years.
explanations.B: Patients with bipolar disorder may gamble and spend large sums of money during a manic episode. Mania, however, is episodic and unlikely to be persistent over 21 year. Diagnosis requires the presence of other manic symptoms, including increased energy, general decreased need for sleep (not associated only with gambling), increased goal-oriented activity, flight of ideas, and pressured speech.
explanations.C: Cyclothymic disorder is characterized by >2 years of cyclical mood disturbances characterized by periods of hypomanic and depressive symptoms that do not meet the full criteria for hypomanic or depressive episodes. Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) involves a chronically depressed mood for >2 years. This patient's moods are related to his gambling behavior (eg, excitement and overconfidence while gambling followed by dysphoria and irritability).
explanations.D: Gambling disorder is defined as persistent and maladaptive gambling behavior that results in impairment or distress. It is considered a nonsubstance behavioral addiction, implying many shared features (eg, anticipatory craving, chronic relapsing course) with substance use disorders.
explanations.E: This patient's grandiose beliefs that he can win money are typical of gambling disorder. Narcissistic personality disorder is characterized by a pattern of grandiosity that is more pervasive in nature, as well as by a need to be the center of attention and admired.
explanations.F: Cyclothymic disorder is characterized by >2 years of cyclical mood disturbances characterized by periods of hypomanic and depressive symptoms that do not meet the full criteria for hypomanic or depressive episodes. Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) involves a chronically depressed mood for >2 years. This patient's moods are related to his gambling behavior (eg, excitement and overconfidence while gambling followed by dysphoria and irritability).

generalExplanation: Gambling disorder is defined as persistent and maladaptive gambling behavior that results in impairment or distress. It is considered a nonsubstance behavioral addiction, implying many shared features (eg, anticipatory craving, chronic relapsing course) with substance use disorders. Mood symptoms related to gambling behavior (ie, irritability, feeling "a little down") are common, as seen in this patient. The diagnosis requires 24 characteristics related to problematic gambling behavior. This patient exhibits the following 4: preoccupation with gambling, frequent return to gambling to attempt to recover past losses, tendency to damage relationships or jeopardize employment, and reliance on others to make up for financial losses. Additional criteria listed in DSM-5 include: gambling when distressed, depressed, or anxious; increased gambling to achieve the desired excitement; irritability/distress when trying to cut back on gambling; and repeated, unsuccessful attempts to cut back on and conceal the extent of the behaviors. Treatment approaches include cognitive-behavioral therapies and participation in self-help programs (eg, Gamblers Anonymous).
educationalObjective: Gambling disorder is characterized by persistent and recurrent maladaptive gambling behavior that results

stem: A 17-year-old boy comes to the office at his father's insistence due to a change in behavior. Ever since his girlfriend ended their relationship last month, the patient has been unable to complete his schoolwork and is uninterested in playing the sports he previously enjoyed. He spends most of his time in his room and refuses to come out for meals. The patient says, "It's too much effort to even get out of bed. I thought everything was going well, and suddenly she just ended it. I don't want to go to school and see her ever again." On further questioning, the patient reports that he has trouble falling asleep and keeps checking his ex-girlfriend's social media posts to see what she is doing in the evenings. He has thought about hanging himself with rope his father keeps in the garage. He has not spoken to anyone else about his suicidal thoughts and does not know if he will act on them. The patient says, "I tried to tell my best friend how I feel, but he just told me to 'get over her.' He doesn't understand and neither will my parents. Please don't tell my parents what I am going through." Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action for this patient?

options.A: Encourage the patient to inform his parents and refer them for family therapy to facilitate the discussion
options.B: Explain the need for breaking confidentiality and hospitalize the patient if his parents give consent
options.C: Inform the parents about the patient's suicidal thoughts and hospitalize him immediately with or without parental consent
options.D: Inform the parents about the patient's suicidal thoughts and instruct them to remove the rope and supervise him until follow-up is arranged
options.E: Maintain confidentiality about the patient's suicidal wishes and hospitalize him with or without parental consent
options.F: Maintain confidentiality and refer for an urgent outpatient psychiatric evaluation

explanations.A: Although the patient should be encouraged to tell his parents what is going on, family therapy can take time and his risk of suicide is high. He must be hospitalized immediately for safety.
explanations.B: Although it is best to treat adolescents with the family's support of the treatment, parental consent is not required for emergency hospitalization.
explanations.C: This patient is severely depressed, has suicidal ideation with thoughts about hanging himself, and may have intent to act on these thoughts. Although confidentiality should be maintained whenever possible to facilitate rapport and encourage trust, if an adolescent patient is at risk of harm to self or others, safety becomes more important and confidentiality must be broken in order to facilitate treatment.
explanations.D: Asking the parents to remove the rope is important, and this needs to be done before the patient is discharged from the hospital. However, sending the patient home with supervision is unsafe and places an unfair burden on the family.
explanations.E: In cases where there is risk of harm, confidentiality should not be maintained. The parents should be informed.
explanations.F: This patient is expressing suicidal ideation with a plan and possible intent and needs emergency hospitalization for his safety. Scheduling an urgent psychiatric evaluation would be appropriate if he were not actively suicidal.

generalExplanation: This patient is severely depressed, has suicidal ideation with thoughts about hanging himself, and may have intent to act on these thoughts. Although confidentiality should be maintained whenever possible to facilitate rapport and encourage trust, if an adolescent patient is at risk of harm to self or others, safety becomes more important and confidentiality must be broken in order to facilitate treatment. Due to his high risk of self-harm, the parents should be informed and the patient should be hospitalized immediately so that he can be closely monitored and placed on suicide precautions. This should preferably be done with parental consent and support, but if necessary it can be done on an involuntarily basis.
educationalObjective: A teenager with active suicidal ideation must be hospitalized for safety and the parents must be informed. Parental consent is ideal but not required for hospitalization.

stem: A 60-year-old woman comes to the office for follow-up of chronic tension-type headaches. Her headaches have not improved after several trials of medications, including those recommended by a neurologist specializing in the management of headaches. The patient says, "I'm really not surprised that this last medication didn't work either. All these drug companies just want to make money. I doubt that anything will help." When asked if she would consider pursuing biofeedback, relaxation training, or stress management therapy, she responds, "There's no point —how can I relax or do therapy when my head is pounding?" The patient's other medical problems include hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, which are well controlled with medication. She has a history of depression following her divorce in her 40s but was unwilling to take an antidepressant or see a counselor at that time. Which of the following statements is the most appropriate response to this patient's concerns?

options.A: I am concerned that depression is contributing to your hopelessness about getting better.
options.B: I can see that it has been frustrating, but let's explore why you seem to reject every new suggestion.
options.C: I can see that you are feeling hopeless; talking with a counselor may help improve your outlook.
options.D: I can see that your lack of improvement has been frustrating; let's identify a small goal we can agree on.
options.E: I share your frustration; let's obtain a second opinion from a psychiatrist who may help identify new I treatment strategies.
options.F: It must be frustrating that medications have not helped; I encourage you to reconsider biofeedback and I relaxation training.

explanations.A: There is insufficient information on this patient to diagnose depression, and she would likely reject this explanation of her poor response. She has previously rejected counseling and is currently resistant to other treatment approaches; therefore, she is unlikely to agree to counseling at this stage.
explanations.B: This statement attempts to confront this patient by pointing out her help-rejecting pattern of behavior. This would likely be perceived as judgmental, resulting in loss of rapport and defensiveness. However, it could be useful as part of a therapeutic intervention by a skilled therapist in the context of structured psychotherapy.
explanations.C: There is insufficient information on this patient to diagnose depression, and she would likely reject this explanation of her poor response. She has previously rejected counseling and is currently resistant to other treatment approaches; therefore, she is unlikely to agree to counseling at this stage.
explanations.D: This patient remains symptomatic despite the best efforts of the physician to treat her with multiple medication trials, and she rejects all recommended nonpharmacological approaches. Such patients believe that no treatment will help and appear not to want to improve.
explanations.E: The understandable tendency to want to refer this patient to another provider or specialist should be avoided (Choice E).
explanations.F: The physician has already encouraged the patient to consider nonpharmacological approaches. Rather than continuing to make treatment recommendations that will likely be rejected, the physician should develop a collaborative focus on a small goal that she identifies.

generalExplanation: This patient remains symptomatic despite the best efforts of the physician to treat her with multiple medication trials, and she rejects all recommended nonpharmacological approaches. Such patients believe that no treatment will help and appear not to want to improve. They are often frustrating to manage and can leave the physician feeling angry and manipulated. The understandable tendency to want to refer this patient to another provider or specialist should be avoided (Choice E). These patients often have underlying depression but will refuse referral to a psychiatrist. They are needy for attention and unconsciously wish to remain symptomatic so that they can continue to see a physician. The best approach is to empathize with them and attempt to engage them in a collaborative plan in which there is mutual agreement about realistic treatment approaches and limited expectations. Empathizing with the patient's frustration over disappointing outcomes and focusing on alleviation of symptoms rather than a cure is often helpful.
educationalObjective: Help-rejecting patients who are hopeless about treatment can lead the physician to become frustrated and confrontational and to desire to refer the patient to another provider. Clear expression of empathy and a collaborative approach with limited goals are the most effective approaches.

stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office due to insomnia and fatigue. She is accompanied by her husband, who is concerned that his wife is exhausted and seems overwhelmed by the responsibilities of being a new mother. The patient had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and took an extended maternity leave to care for their daughter, who is now 3 months old. The patient feels very tired because she awakens early at 4:00 AM and is unable to return to sleep. She frequently lies awake in bed and worries that she is a bad mother. During the day she has little energy and forces herself to take showers and care for the baby. Physical examination is unremarkable. The patient appears sad but says, "I'm sure I would feel better if I could just get some rest." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

options.A: Advise the husband to obtain additional childcare support
options.B: Ask for permission to speak with the husband alone to obtain further information
options.C: Ask the patient about suicidal thoughts
options.D: Prescribe a short course of sleep medication and follow up in 1-2 weeks
options.E: Reassure the patient and husband that she has postpartum blues, which should resolve shortly
options.F: Refer the patient to a support group for new mothers

stem: A 37-year-old man is brought to the emergency department (ED). Police found the patient running into traffic, yelling obscenities at drivers, slamming his body against passing cars, and trying to break windshields with a beer bottle. A witness described him as having "crazy rage." In the ED, the patient remains combative with police and 4 officers are needed to restrain him. He is disoriented, continues to yell, and appears to be responding to internal stimuli. Temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), blood pressure is 190/96 mm Hg, pulse is 142/min, and respirations are 20/min. Examination shows clear lung fields. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Extraocular movements and cranial nerves are intact. Upper and lower limb deep tendon reflexes are 3+ bilaterally. Serum laboratory results are normal and urine toxicology is negative. While in the ED, the patient has a seizure and is treated with benzodiazepines for both the seizure and the agitation. He is admitted to the medical service and treated supportively. The patient remains psychotic for the next 2 days, but his symptoms then begin to subside and eventually resolve. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's presentation?

explanations.A: Brief psychotic disorder may be diagnosed in patients who exhibit >1 day but <1 month of psychotic symptoms (eg, hallucinations, delusions) only if the symptoms are not better explained by substance intoxication/withdrawal, another psychiatric condition, or a medical condition. This patient's presentation is better explained by synthetic cathinone intoxication.
explanations.B: Cannabis intoxication is characterized by euphoria with inappropriate laughter, lethargy, distorted sensory perceptions, conjunctival injection, and increased appetite. It is unlikely to have caused this patient's extreme and extended agitation and delirium and would not explain his hyperreflexia and autonomic hyperactivity. Furthermore, cannabis would be detected on a urine toxicology screen and this patient's screen was negative.
explanations.C: Cocaine intoxication may cause agitation and psychosis; however, compared with the symptoms of bath salt intoxication, the symptoms of cocaine intoxication are less severe and of shorter duration. Routine toxicology screens typically test for cocaine.
explanations.D: MDMA, commonly known as "ecstasy," also has amphetamine-like effects and may lead to delirium and seizures, but it often causes increased feelings of euphoria and intimacy, not combative agitation. In addition, significant hyperthermia may occur in severe MDMA intoxication.
explanations.E: Phencyclidine (PCP) intoxication typically presents with psychomotor agitation, combative behavior, diminished pain perception, hallucinations, hypertension, tachycardia, and multidirectional nystagmus. Compared with the symptoms of synthetic cathinone intoxication, the symptoms of PCP intoxication are usually of shorter duration. In addition, PCP is included in standard urine toxicology screens. This patient has normal extraocular movements and his urine toxicology screen is negative for PCP.
explanations.F: Synthetic cathinones, commonly referred to as "bath salts," consist of a large family of amphetamine analogs. As such, they may increase the release, or inhibit the reuptake, of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin.

generalExplanation: Synthetic cathinones, commonly referred to as "bath salts," consist of a large family of amphetamine analogs. As such, they may increase the release, or inhibit the reuptake, of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin. Symptoms of intoxication include severe agitation, combativeness, psychosis, delirium, myoclonus, and, rarely, seizures. Increased sympathetic outflow may lead to significantly increased blood pressure and heart rate. The most distinguishing feature of synthetic cathinone intoxication is the prolonged duration of effect. Delirium and psychosis due to synthetic cathinones may last up to a week, whereas the effects of intoxication with other amphetamines or hallucinogens are usually of much shorter duration. Synthetic cathinones are usually sold as a white powder in small packages labeled as "bath salts," "plant food," "cleaners," or other substances. Synthetic cathinones may be ingested orally, inhaled, or injected. They are not related to the product Epsom salts or any other substances used in bathing. Routine urine toxicology screens cannot detect synthetic cathinones.

stem: An 18-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after having a seizure in day care. The staff reports that "she suddenly fell down and started shaking," but they also note that the patient has seemed quieter and has repeatedly pulled at her hair over the past month. The patient's mother says, "My daughter used to say 'mama' and 'papa' and babble away but has begun to talk less in the past few months. She's also become more needy, wanting me to feed her rather than using a spoon herself." Medical history is significant for 3 ear infections in the past year and another seizure thought to have been febrile in origin. Family history is significant for early-onset Alzheimer disease in the patient's paternal grandfather and retinoblastoma in a paternal cousin. The patient is afebrile, and other vital signs are normal. On physical examination, the patient makes eye contact with the physician but speaks no words. She is noted to have a lurching gait. Which of the following would most likely establish a diagnosis in this patient?

stem: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his girlfriend after sustaining a hand injury. The two were waiting for a table at a crowded bar when the hostess inadvertently seated another couple that was behind them in line. The patient suddenly became enraged, started pacing back and forth, shouted at the hostess that she was "stupid and incompetent," and threw a nearby chair against the wall, causing damage to the wall and injuring his own hand. He is remorseful about his behavior, but his girlfriend says, "He can be moody, frequently gets defensive, and loses his temper with the slightest provocation." They have had several heated arguments during which he has thrown and broken objects. The patient has no medical history. Physical examination is unremarkable except for swelling and lacerations of the hand. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

explanations.A: Although aggressive behavior is common in antisocial personality disorder, it is often premeditated with the goal of gaining an advantage or intimidating others. Other features of antisocial personality disorder include a pervasive pattern of breaking laws, deceiving others, behaving irresponsibly, and lacking remorse.
explanations.B: Patients with bipolar disorder may have aggressive outbursts during a manic episode. However, manic episodes usually last days to months (unlike IED episodes, which last <30 minutes). In addition, this patient does not have other key manic symptoms (eg, elevated mood, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech).
explanations.C: Patients with borderline personality disorder may exhibit inappropriate anger and rages, but these outbursts typically occur in the context of an unstable relationship and are related to underlying fears of abandonment. This patient lacks other characteristic borderline features (eg, suicidal behavior, chronic feelings of emptiness, abandonment fears).
explanations.D: Although disruptive mood dysregulation disorder may also present with disproportionate verbal or physical outbursts, diagnosis requires onset before age 10 and persistent irritability or anger between episodes. The diagnosis is not made after age 18.
explanations.E: This patient's pattern of impulsive, aggressive behavior is suggestive of intermittent explosive disorder (IED), an impulse control disorder. Patients with IED are unable to restrain their aggressive impulses, resulting in verbal or physical aggression that is out of proportion to the provocation.
explanations.F: Although substance intoxication is associated with aggressive behavior, this patient's pattern of short- lived episodes and lack of signs of intoxication on examination is more consistent with IED.

generalExplanation: This patient's pattern of impulsive, aggressive behavior is suggestive of intermittent explosive disorder (IED), an impulse control disorder. Patients with IED are unable to restrain their aggressive impulses, resulting in verbal or physical aggression that is out of proportion to the provocation. The violent, impulsive outburst is typically preceded by rising tension that escalates rapidly to a state of rage without thought to the consequences of the behavior. Episodes last <30 minutes and may provide an immediate sense of relief, usually followed by remorse, dysphoria, and embarrassment. Significant functional impairment due to interpersonal difficulties, job loss, school suspension, and legal problems is common. IED tends to be chronic and is associated with high rates of psychiatric comorbidity. It should not be diagnosed if the impulsive, aggressive behavior occurs exclusively in the context of another active psychiatric disorder (eg, acute manic episode in bipolar disorder). Treatment consists of cognitive-behavioral therapy and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
educationalObjective: Intermittent explosive disorder is characterized by recurrent episodes of impulsive verbal or physical aggression. The aggressive behaviors are unplanned and out of proportion to the provocation.

stem: A 44-year-old man comes to the office due to depression, loss of interest, impaired concentration, fatigue, and poor sleep. The patient is not suicidal and has no psychotic symptoms. He has no psychiatric history. Physical examination and laboratory evaluation are unremarkable. Major depressive disorder is diagnosed, and he is treated with 50 mg of sertraline. After a month of antidepressant treatment, the patient reports improvement in his energy level and sleep, although he continues to struggle with some sadness and low motivation. The dose of sertraline is increased to 100 mg. At his 2-month follow-up, the patient has no depressive symptoms and says, "I feel like I'm totally back to normal. Work is going well and I'm really enjoying life again." He has no adverse effects from the sertraline. The patient asks when he can stop taking the medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

stem: A 43-year-old woman presents to the emergency department complaining of feeling "horrible." She has not been sleeping through the night, has been losing weight, and has crying fits throughout the day. These symptoms began about 3 months ago when she discovered that her husband was having an affair. She feels betrayed and foolish for having failed to recognize it sooner. She states that she has been doubting her abilities as a wife and mother. She has also stopped participating in her weekly book club and has not returned phone calls from friends and family recently, preferring to keep to herself instead. She says she "just can't take the embarrassment" and has been having frequent thoughts of suicide. The patient has been drinking 2-3 glasses of wine to help her fall asleep at night and using marijuana several times a month. She has no psychiatric history. Physical examination is unremarkable. stem: A 37-year-old man comes to the emergency department for evaluation of back pain. The patient was seen 2 days ago in the emergency department for similar pain symptoms and was discharged on naproxen. Medical history is significant for asthma, hepatitis C, and opioid use disorder. Temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), blood pressure is 138/92 mm Hg, and pulse is 104/min. The patient is irritable while his vital signs are being taken and angrily says to the nurse, "That medication I got was useless. My pain is now 10 times worse." stem: A 75-year-old man is brought to the office by his wife due to worsening psychosis. The patient has a history of Parkinson disease treated with carbidopa-levodopa and pramipexole. Dosages of both medications were increased 6 months ago to target worsening tremor and bradykinesia, resulting in significant improvement in motor symptoms. However, over the ensuing months, the patient began experiencing paranoia and hallucinations. He has been verbally assaultive toward the mail carrier, claiming that she is stealing from him. The patient has also been observed talking to himself and is often distracted by visual stimuli that are invisible to others. Dose reduction of his antiparkinson medications resulted in significant rebound motor symptoms, requiring resumption of the prereduction doses. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 118/82 mm Hg, and pulse is 62/min. The patient appears suspicious of the examiner and mumbles to himself throughout the examination. Mild rigidity, tremor, and gait instability are present. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

explanations.A: Amantadine (an antiviral) and selegiline (a monoamine oxidase inhibitor) are both dopaminergic agents used in the treatment of PD. These drugs would be of little use in this patient given that they are inferior to pramipexole as antiparkinson agents and are also associated with psychosis due to their dopaminergic activity.
explanations.B: Antipsychotics with more potent dopamine-2 receptor antagonism (eg, haloperidol, risperidone) should be avoided as these medications have the highest risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and will worsen Parkinson motor symptoms (Choices B and D).
explanations.C: Psychotic symptoms, most commonly visual hallucinations and paranoid delusions, are a frequent complication of Parkinson disease (PD). They tend to worsen as the underlying disease process progresses and are the strongest predictor of nursing home placement.

generalExplanation: Psychotic symptoms, most commonly visual hallucinations and paranoid delusions, are a frequent complication of Parkinson disease (PD). They tend to worsen as the underlying disease process progresses and are the strongest predictor of nursing home placement. Although PD psychosis can occur as a result of the underlying disease process, the risk increases in patients treated with dopaminergic medications. Dopamine agonists (eg, pramipexole, ropinirole) are associated with a greater risk of psychosis than the dopamine precursor and gold- standard antiparkinson medication, carbidopa-levodopa. Treatment of PD psychosis may involve a dose reduction of antiparkinson medication, medication substitution, and/or the addition of a low-potency antipsychotic medication. When antiparkinson medication adjustments fail, as in this patient, a trial of an antipsychotic is warranted. Low-potency antipsychotics with minimal dopamine-2 receptor antagonism such as quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin are preferred. Antipsychotics with more potent dopamine-2 receptor antagonism (eg, haloperidol, risperidone) should be avoided as these medications have the highest risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and will worsen Parkinson motor symptoms (Choices B and D).

stem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the office due to unusual behavior. The patient's mother reports that his behavior began to change 2 months ago, when he started withdrawing from his friends and losing interest in his classes and school activities. During this time, his grades declined, and he spent hours each day developing a code in which certain colors had specific, personal meanings. His mother says, "He insists on wearing the same blue shirt every day. He doesn't even wash it anymore." The patient refuses to ride in the family's gray car because "only primary colors are good." His mother has heard him talking to himself late at night and worries that he is not getting enough sleep. The patient does not use alcohol or illicit drugs. Medical and family history are unremarkable. Vital signs are within normal limits. The patient is tracking appropriately on growth curves. On physical examination, the patient is wearing a stained blue shirt and jeans. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal, and the abdomen is soft and nontender with no hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic examination is unremarkable. The patient makes minimal eye contact and is slow to respond, but he becomes eager to describe his color system when asked about it. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?

explanations.A: Although this patient has fixated interests characteristic of an autism spectrum disorder, symptoms of autism are usually recognized by age 2 and include chronic deficits in social communication and repetitive behaviors. It would not explain this patient's recent social withdrawal and development of psychosis.
explanations.B: Brief psychotic disorder is diagnosed when positive psychotic symptoms last 21 day and <1 month. It is characterized by a sudden onset and a full return to premorbid level of functioning.
explanations.C: Delusional disorder is characterized by 21 delusion in the absence of other psychotic symptoms. Functioning may be normal apart from the direct impact of the delusion.
explanations.D: Although obsessive-compulsive disorder can present with obsessions related to color coding, these obsessions do not appear to be associated with a feared event or anxiety in this patient (who is eager to discuss his color system). In addition, his negative symptoms, possible hallucinations, and progressive functional impairment are more consistent with schizophreniform disorder.

In this patient, the abrupt onset and short-lived timeline of symptoms make a personality disorder unlikely and are more consistent with schizophreniform disorder.

Schizophreniform disorder is diagnosed when the symptoms of schizophrenia are present for ≥1 month but <6 months. These symptoms include ≥2 of the following: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms. Impairment in functioning may be present but is not required for the diagnosis. The diagnosis of schizophreniform disorder is made provisionally; if symptoms persist 26 months, the diagnosis is changed to schizophrenia. educationalObjective: Schizophreniform disorder is differentiated from schizophrenia by the duration of symptoms. In schizophreniform disorder, symptoms must last for ≥1 month but <6 months. The diagnosis of schizophrenia requires symptoms to persist for 26 months.

She has a history of 2 depressive episodes previously treated with fluoxetine and venlafaxine but currently takes no psychiatric medications. Physical examination is remarkable for 4.53 kg (10 lb) weight loss. Laboratory results are within normal limits. On mental status examination, the patient whispers and is slow to respond. She says, "My body is infected with worms." She has no suicidal ideation but says, "I deserve to die; my body is decaying from the inside anyway." Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

explanations.A: Antipsychotic monotherapy (eg, aripiprazole, quetiapine) or antidepressant monotherapy (eg, mirtazapine, venlafaxine) is not as effective as combination therapy. Patients with MDD with psychotic features should be treated with a combination of an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic.
explanations.B: The combination of 2 antidepressants (the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor antidepressant, escitalopram, with the dopamine-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, bupropion) can be considered for the management of nonpsychotic depression that does not respond to monotherapy alone. However, it would not treat this patient's psychosis.
explanations.C: The combination of an antidepressant (eg, fluoxetine) and lithium is used in the management of treatment-resistant, nonpsychotic depression and bipolar disorder. It is not an effective combination for MDD with psychosis.
explanations.D: Antipsychotic monotherapy (eg, aripiprazole, quetiapine) or antidepressant monotherapy (eg, mirtazapine, venlafaxine) is not as effective as combination therapy. Patients with MDD with psychotic features should be treated with a combination of an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic.

generalExplanation: This patient's worsening depression and development of delusions are consistent with major depressive disorder (MDD) with psychotic features. MDD with psychotic features is a severe subtype of depression characterized by delusions and/or hallucinations. Psychotic features typically have depressive themes such as guilt, worthlessness, and dying (eg, this patient's delusions that her body is decaying and that she deserves to die). Accurate diagnosis is important because treatment of MDD with psychotic features differs from treatment of nonpsychotic depression (antidepressant monotherapy). First-line treatment consists of an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic (eg, sertraline and risperidone). Electroconvulsive therapy is another first-line option, but it is typically reserved for patients who require rapid response due to severe suicidality or refusal to eat or drink.
educationalObjective: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features is a subtype of depression characterized by severe depression and delusions and/or hallucinations. First-line treatment consists of an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic or electroconvulsive therapy.

stem: A 19-year-old man is brought to the office by his mother due to sad mood and declining grades at college. Previously a straight-A student, he is now getting Cs and Ds, and his mother worries he will not complete his freshman year. The patient says, "I feel depressed and hopeless about the future." He has little interest in his classes, has difficulty concentrating on assignments, and abruptly decided to quit the soccer team. He refuses to answer any phone calls from his friends and keeps himself isolated at home. The patient feels that there is little point in living but has no suicidal intent or plan. He has tried alcohol at parties on 2 occasions but does not use illicit drugs. There is no history of mania. There is a family history of untreated depression in his mother and grandmother. Physical examination and laboratory values are normal. Major depressive disorder is diagnosed, and treatment is discussed. The patient is willing to take medication, but his mother is concerned that antidepressants can cause people to become suicidal. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to the mother?

options.A: Due to the slightly increased risk of suicidal thoughts in adolescents, antidepressants are prescribed only for patients who fail psychotherapy.
options.B: Some classes of antidepressants have a lower risk of increasing suicidal thoughts, and for adolescents we prescribe those first.
options.C: There is a slightly increased risk of suicidal thoughts in young people treated with antidepressants, but only in those under age 18.
options.D: There is no association between antidepressants and an increased risk of suicidal thoughts in I adolescents.
options.E: The slightly increased risk of suicidal thoughts with antidepressants in this age group needs to be I weighed against the risk of completed suicide in untreated depression. I Submit I

explanations.A: Antidepressant treatment should not be withheld due to this concern or limited to patients who have failed psychotherapy (Choice A).
explanations.B: Although some antidepressants are avoided as first-line agents due to their adverse side-effect profile, there is no known or clear difference in the risk of suicidal thoughts or behaviors among different classes of antidepressants. All adolescents started on an antidepressant should be monitored closely.
explanations.C: The warning is applicable to all patients under age 25 years, not just those under age 18.
explanations.D: The warning was based on studies showing a slightly increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors (not completed suicide) among a small group of child and adolescent patients treated with antidepressants compared with placebo (Choice D).
explanations.E: In 2007 the US Food and Drug Administration extended its warning that all patients age <25 should be informed about the small risk of becoming suicidal during initial antidepressant treatment. The warning was based on studies showing a slightly increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors (not completed suicide) among a small group of child and adolescent patients treated with antidepressants compared with placebo (Choice D).

generalExplanation: In 2007 the US Food and Drug Administration extended its warning that all patients age <25 should be informed about the small risk of becoming suicidal during initial antidepressant treatment. The warning was based on studies showing a slightly increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors (not completed suicide) among a small group of child and adolescent patients treated with antidepressants compared with placebo (Choice D). Decisions regarding prescribing antidepressants for adolescents must weigh the risk of antidepressant-related suicidal thoughts and behaviors against the established benefits of antidepressants and the long-term risk of completed suicide in untreated depression. Although there is ongoing debate about the evidence for a link between antidepressants and suicidality, the consensus among experts and in practice guidelines is that the benefits of antidepressants for moderate to severe depression outweigh the risks. Antidepressant treatment should not be withheld due to this concern or limited to patients who have failed psychotherapy (Choice A). Physicians should closely monitor patients for increasing suicidal thoughts and behaviors, especially following initiation of antidepressant treatment.
educationalObjective: The slightly increased risk of antidepressant-related suicidal thoughts and behaviors in some children and adolescents must be weighed against the efficacy of antidepressants and the risk of completed suicide in depression. Patients should be carefully monitored for suicidality at the beginning of antidepressant therapy.

These findings are consistent with neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), an idiosyncratic drug reaction to dopamine antagonists. Although symptoms of NMS typically begin within 2 weeks of initiation of the precipitating agent, they can occur at any time during treatment. Sustained muscle contraction can lead to muscle breakdown that results in many of the observed laboratory abnormalities, including elevated creatine kinase, electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hypocalcemia, metabolic acidosis), and elevated blood urea nitrogen and creatinine (ie, acute Kidney Injury due to rhabdomyolysis). Nonspecific laboratory abnormalities can include leukocytosis with a left shift, slight protein elevation in the cerebrospinal fluid (possibly reflecting increased neurometabolites), and elevated liver enzymes. Discontinuation of the antipsychotic is the single most important intervention. Additional treatment often includes hydration (eg, intravenous fluids), cooling, and medications to control agitation (eg, benzodiazepines) and decrease muscle contraction (eg, benzodiazepines, dantrolene).
educationalObjective: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome typically presents with altered mental status, fever, neuromuscular abnormalities (eg, muscular rigidity), and autonomic instability. The most critical intervention is cessation of antipsychotic medications.

stem: A 23-year-old woman comes to the office due to skin concerns. The patient states, "I have pockmarks on my nose from having acne as a teenager." She has tried high-dose retinol creams and skin-resurfacing procedures with no improvement. The patient applies concealer to her nose every morning and has been late to work multiple times due to her routine. She touches up her makeup throughout the day and is concerned that her supervisor has started to notice her frequent trips to the bathroom. Vital signs are within normal limits. Skin examination shows pores of minimal size, if any, on the nose and forehead; no acne or scarring is visible. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate statement?

options.A: "It's common to feel self-conscious about appearance from time to time, but your skin looks healthy and normal."
options.B: "Nasal skin can be a problem area for lots of people; has anything you've tried in the past been helpful for your skin?"
options.C: "Skin can be irritated by recurrent makeup applications; I recommend applying only moisturizer and sunscreen to see if that helps." I
options.D: "You have concerns about how your nose appears; if we were to ask other people about your nose, I what would they say?"
options.E: "Your skin does not seem to have any scarring on examination; is it possible that these appearance I flaws are only noticeable to you?"

explanations.A: Patients with BDD are rarely reassured when told that their appearance is normal. They may feel that such statements minimize or ignore their concerns.
explanations.B: This statement both validates the patient's concerns (by normalizing preoccupations about nasal skin) and inquires about past treatments, making it seem as if the physician agrees that something is wrong with her appearance. This approach may inadvertently reinforce her concerns.
explanations.C: Applying only moisturizer and sunscreen does not address the underlying issue of BDD, so this recommendation is unlikely to be helpful to the patient. It is also misleading to describe the patient's skin as irritated when examination shows no abnormalities.
explanations.D: Body dysmorphic disorder e Preoccupation with 21 perceived physical defects e Defects not observable or appear slight to others -_ e Repetitive behavior performed in response to the preoccupation (eg, mirror Clinical features . : ; ; fo aha checking, concealing, excessive grooming, skin picking) e Significant distress or impairment e Variable insight (good, poor, absent/delusional beliefs) e Acknowledge distress; do not refer to perceived flaws as "imagined" : e Reassurance about normal appearance rarely helpful Approach to patient ee : i : k e Focus on alleviating distress & functional impairment e Avoid inappropriate cosmetic/medical/surgical treatments e Antidepressants (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) Treatment eo : ¢ Cognitive-behavioral therapy This patient's excessive preoccupation with a slight or nonexistent defect in physical appearance (ie, belief that her nose is scarred from acne) is consistent with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD).
explanations.E: This statement directly challenges the patient's perception of her appearance, which is likely counterproductive to developing a collaborative physician-patient relationship.

generalExplanation: Body dysmorphic disorder e Preoccupation with 21 perceived physical defects e Defects not observable or appear slight to others -_ e Repetitive behavior performed in response to the preoccupation (eg, mirror Clinical features . : ; ; fo aha checking, concealing, excessive grooming, skin picking) e Significant distress or impairment e Variable insight (good, poor, absent/delusional beliefs) e Acknowledge distress; do not refer to perceived flaws as "imagined" : e Reassurance about normal appearance rarely helpful Approach to patient ee : i : k e Focus on alleviating distress & functional impairment e Avoid inappropriate cosmetic/medical/surgical treatments e Antidepressants (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) Treatment eo : ¢ Cognitive-behavioral therapy This patient's excessive preoccupation with a slight or nonexistent defect in physical appearance (ie, belief that her nose is scarred from acne) is consistent with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). In response to appearance concerns, patients with BDD engage in time-consuming behaviors, such as this patient repeatedly examining her appearance in the mirror and reapplying makeup to conceal her perceived defects. Patients with BDD typically have limited insight into their condition and therefore require a sensitive and tactful assessment approach. The physician should acknowledge their distress and avoid referring to perceived defects as "imagined" or arguing with them about their appearance. Physicians should empathize with patients' efforts to cope with their condition and determine their level of insight by gently exploring their perceptions of how others see them. In BDD, insight can range from fair to good (patient acknowledges beliefs about appearance are possibly or probably not true) to poor to absent (patient thinks beliefs about appearance are probably or definitely true).
educationalObjective: Body dysmorphic disorder is characterized by preoccupation with slight to nonexistent appearance flaws and related repetitive behaviors such as checking, comparing with others, and camouflaging the perceived defect. Assessment requires a sensitive approach that acknowledges patients' distress and explores the level of their insight while avoiding direct confrontation or referring to perceived defects as "imagined."

stem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the office due to insomnia and depressed mood. She describes feeling angry and sad since her husband of 35 years unexpectedly announced that he wanted a divorce 2 months ago. She says, "I was devastated because I thought we had a pretty good marriage, better than most. My whole life has been turned upside down. I can't even think about going on dates at my age." The patient stays up well past her usual bedtime worrying about living alone and supporting herself financially. She recently started drinking wine before bedtime to help her fall asleep. Although she was regularly eating lunch with friends, she has canceled multiple times because she "can't bear to go through the whole story again and again." She has no suicidal ideation. The patient is tearful when discussing the divorce but brightens when asked about her grandchildren. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Acute stress disorder is characterized by reexperiencing events (ie, intrusive memories, flashbacks), avoidance, negative mood, dissociation, and hyperarousal lasting from 3 days to 1 month following a life- threatening traumatic event.
explanations.B: Differential diagnosis of depressed mood e ≥2 weeks . .
explanations.C: Generalized anxiety disorder is characterized by excessive worry over multiple issues lasting 26 months.
explanations.D: This patient's insomnia developed in response to a stressor. It is better explained as part of an adjustment disorder and would not be diagnosed separately.
explanations.E: A diagnosis of major depressive disorder requires a 2-week period of ≥5 of 9 symptoms: depressed mood, decreased interest/pleasure, appetite disturbance, sleep disturbance, psychomotor agitation/retardation, loss of energy, excessive guilt, impaired concentration, and suicidal ideation.

This patient's onset of depressive symptoms following the major life stressor of divorce and the absence of symptoms severe enough to diagnose major depressive disorder make adjustment disorder with depressed mood the most likely diagnosis. Adjustment disorder involves emotional or behavioral symptoms (eg, depression, anxiety, disturbance of conduct) developing within 3 months of an identifiable stressor and lasting <6 months once the stressor or its consequences ceases. Symptoms in an adjustment disorder must be distressing and/or impairing (eg, this patient is distressed and seeking treatment) but are insufficient to meet full criteria for another mental disorder such as major depressive disorder. This patient has sadness, anxiety, and sleep disturbance related to the divorce and living alone. However, she does not experience the pervasive sadness, anhedonia, guilt, impaired concentration, appetite disturbance, psychomotor changes, or suicidality that characterize major depressive disorder.
educationalObjective: Adjustment disorder involves symptoms occurring within 3 months of an identifiable stressor that cause significant distress and/or impairment. It is not diagnosed if a patient meets diagnostic criteria for another mental disorder.

stem: A6-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother due to learning difficulties at school. The patient was adopted from an overseas orphanage at age 5 and stayed home until beginning kindergarten 6 months ago. His birth and developmental history are unknown. Since beginning school, he has struggled to keep up with reading and writing. Educational testing was completed and showed an intelligence quotient (IQ) of 68. Audiology revealed a mild conductive hearing loss in his right ear. The patient's mother says, "He is a really happy kid and enjoys playing with his older siblings. I know he doesn't talk as much as other kids his age, but I thought that would improve with time." Vital signs are within normal limits; weight and height curves are at the 70th and 10th percentiles, respectively. The patient is sitting on the floor playing with a range of toys. Physical examination is significant for a flat nasal bridge and a grade 3 holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border. He makes eye contact, has a friendly demeanor, and responds to questions with 3- to 4-word phrases. Which of the following tests is most likely to reveal the diagnosis?

This patient with learning difficulties and a low intelligence quotient (1Q) has intellectual disability. In the setting of dysmorphic features or a family history of intellectual disability, a genetic cause should be suspected. In this case, the most likely cause is Down syndrome, the most common chromosomal abnormality associated with intellectual disability. Congenital heart defects (eg, atrioventricular defect, ventricular septal defect [VSD]) occur in 50% of patients; the holosystolic murmur in this case is consistent with a VSD. Hearing impairment due to congenital hearing loss or frequent otitis media is also common. Patients often have a friendly demeanor and poor vertical growth, as seen here. 'The diagnosis Is frequently established based on prenatal testing or characteristic dysmorpnic features at birth (eg, flat nasal bridge). However, in a patient with mosaicism (extra copy of chromosome 21 in some cells), such dysmorphic features may be less prominent and diagnosis may be delayed. A karyotype should be performed; identification of trisomy 21 is diagnostic.
educationalObjective: Down syndrome should be suspected in a child with intellectual disability and characteristic dysmorphic features,

stem: A 76-year-old man is brought to the office by his wife for follow-up of recent behavioral changes. The patient has been much more withdrawn than usual over the past 6 months and often appears sad. He stopped driving a year earlier after getting lost several times in his own neighborhood. He now needs help with grocery shopping, meal preparation, and finances. His wife says, "He has good days and bad days. Sometimes he's almost like his old self; other times, he seems confused." She reports that while the patient sleeps, he frequently seems to act out his dreams and has kicked her on occasion. Medical history includes hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. Temperature is 37.3 C (99.1 F), blood pressure is 137/78 mm Hg, pulse is 78/min, and respirations are 14/min. On neurologic examination, there is bilateral resistance to passive movement of the upper extremities, and the patient walks with an unsteady gait. Montreal cognitive assessment score is 21/30 (normal: ≥26). The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

explanations.A: Alzheimer disease typically presents with early and prominent memory loss. This patient's pattern of early deficits in executive function and visuospatial ability and his core features of fluctuating cognition, RBD, and parkinsonism make DLB more likely.
explanations.B: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a rare prion disease characterized by behavioral changes, rapidly progressive dementia, and myoclonus.
explanations.C: Differential diagnosis of dementia subtypes e Early, insidious short-term E memory loss Alzheimer , , . e Language deficits & spatial disease ee : disorientation e Early personality changes e Apathy, disinhibition & Frontotemporal .
explanations.D: Although depression can present with cognitive impairment, it would not explain this patient's RBD, parkinsonism, and fluctuating cognition.
explanations.E: Frontotemporal dementia is characterized by early personality changes (eg, euphoria, disinhibition, apathy), compulsive behaviors (eg, peculiar eating habits, hyperorality), and impaired memory. Visuospatial functions usually remain intact.
explanations.F: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is characterized by the triad of cognitive changes (eg, decreased attention and concentration, apathy), gait dysfunction, and urinary incontinence.
explanations.G: Vascular dementia is typically associated with focal neurologic findings specific to the location of causal infarct(s) and stepwise decline in function.

' : compulsive behavior dementia e Frontotemporal atrophy on neuroimaging e Visual hallucinations oo. e Spontaneous parkinsonism Dementia with Lewy : ne . e Fluctuating cognition bodies . e Rapid eye movement behavior disorder e Ataxia early in disease Normal pressure I ¢ Urinary incontinence hydrocephalus e Dilated ventricles on neuroimaging e Behavioral changes Prion disease e Rapid progression e Myoclonus &/or seizures This patient's presentation is most consistent with dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). Diagnosis of probable DLB requires the presence of dementia (eg, low Montreal cognitive assessment score) and 2 of 4 additional core features: e parkinsonism (eg, limb rigidity) e fluctuating cognition (eg, "good days and bad days," periodic confusion) e visual hallucinations (occur in 2 of 3 patients, but not required for diagnosis) e rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD). RBD, a parasomnia characterized by dream enactment behavior during loss of normal REM sleep atonia, is a common and early symptom of DLB. Patients often also have early deficits in executive function (eg, needing help with finances, shopping) and visuospatial ability (eg, getting lost in the neighborhood). Depression, as seen in this patient, is common and occurs in most patients at some point in the illness. Other symptoms include dopamine antagonist (eg, antipsychotics) sensitivity, repeated falls, syncope, autonomic dysfunction, and delusions.
educationalObjective: Dementia with Lewy bodies is characterized by early visuospatial and executive dysfunction and at least 2 of 4 additional core features: visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, fluctuating cognition, and rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder. Ss References

stem: A 46-year-old hospitalized man is evaluated for confusion. He was admitted 3 days ago after a motor vehicle collision in which he was a passenger. He sustained fractures of the right tibia and fibula, which were surgically reduced and fixed. The patient had a small subdural hematoma without midline shift, which was managed nonoperatively. He has been receiving intravenous morphine for pain control. This morning, the patient was agitated and disruptive and was talking to persons who were not there. He has no significant medical history and takes no regular medications. Temperature is 37.5 C (99.5 F), blood pressure is 170/100 mm Hg, pulse is 120/min and regular, and respirations are 22/min. Pulse oximetry shows 96% on room air. The patient appears diaphoretic and tremulous and is trying to pull out the intravenous lines. He is not cooperative for funduscopic examination, but pupils are equal and reactive bilaterally. Breath sounds are normal and no heart murmurs are heard. The abdomen is soft and nontender. The surgical incision shows no surrounding erythema. The patient moves all extremities without limitations. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's acute confusion?

explanations.A: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome . .
explanations.B: Elevated intracranial pressure usually manifests with lethargy or obtundation, pupillary abnormalities (eg, enlarged, asymmetric, nonreactive), and Cushing response (eg, hypertension, bradycardia, respiratory depression). Although this patient has a subdural hematoma, he has normal, reactive pupils and is agitated and tachycardic.
explanations.C: Fat embolism syndrome occurs 1-3 days following a traumatic injury with the triad of petechiae, pulmonary infiltrates with hypoxia, and altered mentation. This patient has only altered mentation.
explanations.D: Malignant hyperthermia is an autosomal dominant disorder of skeletal muscle hypermetabolism that leads to hyperpyrexia, muscle rigidity and breakdown, and respiratory and metabolic acidosis. It occurs rarely and usually only perioperatively with exposure to volatile anesthetics and/or succinylcholine.
explanations.E: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a reaction to neuroleptic medications (eg, haloperidol, fluphenazine) that results in severe ("lead pipe") muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, delirium, and autonomic instability. This patient is not on neuroleptic medication and does not have a fever.
explanations.F: Opiate intoxication leads to lethargy, constricted pupils, and respiratory depression.
explanations.G: Pulmonary embolism is a potential postoperative complication usually presenting with chest pain, dyspnea, hypoxia, tachycardia, and diaphoresis. Delirium and agitation would be an uncommon presentation, but this patient is not hypoxemic.

generalExplanation: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome . . : Onset since last Manifestations Symptoms/signs f drink (hr) Mild Anxiety, insomnia, tremors, diaphoresis, palpitations, gastrointestinal 6.24 withdrawal I upset, intact orientation I Seizures Single or multiple generalized tonic-clonic 12-48 Alcoholic , , " : ; aI . __ I Visual, auditory, or tactile; intact orientation; stable vital signs 12-48 hallucinosis Delirium Confusion, agitation, fever, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, 48-96 tremens hallucinations In a patient who has been hospitalized for 72 hours, the onset of acute change in cognition and attention, tachycardia, hypertension, tremulousness, diaphoresis, agitation, and hallucinations should raise suspicion for delirium tremens (U1) due to aicono! withdrawal. Chronic alcohol use results in insensitivity to GABA, the neurotransmitter principally responsible for maintaining inhibitory tone. In contrast, a prolonged decrease in or cessation of alcohol intake leads to disequilibrium between inhibition and excitation, favoring excitation of the central, somatic, and autonomic nervous systems. A history of alcohol consumption may go undetected in patients who have trauma or encephalopathy. Manifestations of withdrawal may be mistaken for symptoms of the concurrent condition or surgery. These manifestations vary based on quantity, duration, and time since the last drink and may include: e Early withdrawal (6-36 hours) - tremor, anxiety, headache, normal sensorium e Neuropsychiatric (12-48 hours) - generalized seizures, hallucinations e DT (48-96 hours) - altered sensorium, agitation, tremor, autonomic instability Management of DT includes ruling out other causes of delirium, providing nutritional and electrolyte supplementation, and administering benzodiazepines.
educationalObjective: Delirium tremens is a severe manifestation of alcohol withdrawal usually presenting 48-96 hours after the last drink. It is defined by autonomic excitation, agitation, tremor, and altered sensorium.

stem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the office by his parents due to concern about a change in his behavior. Over the past 3 months he has become more withdrawn, spending more time alone and turning down opportunities to socialize with his friends. He is frequently moody and irritable. The patient feels unmotivated at school and seems unconcerned that his grades have dropped. His parents believe that his behavior changed after he was rejected by a girl, who subsequently called him a "loser" on social media. When seen alone, the patient says, "! don't think I will ever get over this girl," who he believes was his "soul mate." He uses marijuana occasionally but does not use alcohol. Physical examination is normal apart from a 2.7-kg (6-lb) weight loss since his last visit. He says, "I feel pretty down. I would consider talking to someone or taking medication but don't want to worry my parents." Which of the following is the most appropriate step prior to initiating treatment for this patient?

options.A: Assure the patient that everything he says is confidential
options.B: Discuss the risks and benefits of psychotherapy versus medication
options.C: Encourage the patient to tell his parents how he feels
options.D: Inform the patient that parental permission is needed to prescribe medication
options.E: Inquire if the patient has thoughts of harming himself
options.F: Reassure the patient that sadness is normal after a romantic breakup
options.G: Recommend psychotherapy in addition to medication

explanations.A: Confidentiality should not be promised because it cannot be maintained if there is a concern for safety (Choice A).
explanations.B: Although parental consent is required to prescribe medication, and it is important to respond to this patient's interest in treatment, it is premature to recommend treatment with antidepressants and/or psychotherapy prior to completing a thorough assessment.
explanations.C: Although adolescents should be encouraged to involve their parents in decision-making, the priority in this case is to determine if the patient is a danger to himself. If there is any concern for the patient's safety, the parents must be informed with or without consent.
explanations.D: Although parental consent is required to prescribe medication, and it is important to respond to this patient's interest in treatment, it is premature to recommend treatment with antidepressants and/or psychotherapy prior to completing a thorough assessment.

explanations.F: This patient has had persistent depressive symptoms for 3 months and should not simply be reassured. A thorough evaluation for depression, including careful screening for suicidal thoughts, is necessary.
